newsitem.title: FRANCE: Renault, unions in Vilvoorde outline deal.
newsitem.headline: Renault, unions in Vilvoorde outline deal.

text.p: French carmaker Renault SA said on Thursday it had reached the outlines of a deal with unions under which there would be no immediate forced lay-offs at its doomed assembly plant in Belgium.
Renault managers had been meeting unions in Belgium this week to discuss the closure amid pressure to work out a generous settlement for the 2,900 workers at the Vilvoorde plant.
"There will be no forced redundancies. We are helping people for two years to find a solution," a company spokeswoman said after the deal was hammered out shortly before dawn on Thursday.
Renault, which lost 5.25 billion francs last year, confirmed during the weekend that the Vilvoorde plant would close as part of a restructuring of its ailing car operations.
The first announcement of Renault's plans to close the plant in February caused a wave of protests in France and Belgium.

Renault said Thursday's framework deal, which must be presented to workers on Friday, would give them up to two years to find a job while remaining in "technical unemployment" on compensation of 43,000 Belgian francs a month.
A special unit would be set up to help them find work.
The deal also calls for early retirement for 522 people between the ages of 48 and 50, the spokeswoman said.
Workers taking redundancy would be offered cash bonuses averaging 900,000 Belgian francs and going as high as two million Belgian francs, depending on length of service.
Renault also reiterated plans to set up a new industrial activity at Vilvoorde that would keep on 400 staff.
Renault did not give an estimate for the total cost of the deal to the company.
The carmaker has set aside 2.8 billion French francs to pay for closing Vilvoorde, including the cost of a jobs package, reconstruction of the site and capital losses on investments.
Union representatives who had fought hard to have the plant kept open, grudgingly welcomed the terms of the package.
"There will be 400 jobs, but we regret they will not be industrial jobs," union leader Karel Gacoms told Belgian radio. The radio said the 400 jobs would be mainly in maintenance.
France Inter radio said union leaders were "moderately satisfied" with the deal which had included some concessions.
The deal will help France's recently elected Socialists to draw a line under the Vilvoorde affair, which has sparked some sniping at the government from its own parliamentary benches.

Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, who pledged last month to put pressure on Renault to seek alternatives to closure, is due to appear on television later on Thursday. He is expected to defend his decision to go along with the closure after an independent consultant concluded there were no other possible choices.
Renault is 46 percent owned by the French state.
